notes.h: Classes of retail outlet (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A retail outlet is a business that sells goods to the public. Outlets are grouped into classes by ownership, range of goods and pricing policy, and each class suits a different kind of shopper.
points: Independent retailer: a single, locally owned shop, such as a butcher, jeweller or boutique, offering personal service and a specialised range. Advantage: personal service. Disadvantage: higher prices and a smaller range.

Chain store (multiple retailer): several outlets under one owner, selling a standard range and buying in bulk, such as Penneys or Dunnes Stores. Buying in bulk lets the owner pass on lower costs to shoppers.

Supermarket: a self-service store (shoppers pick items themselves) selling a wide range of food and household goods, such as Tesco, SuperValu or Centra. Advantage: wide range and one-stop shopping. Disadvantage: it is impersonal.
Department store: a large store divided into departments selling clothing, household goods and cosmetics, such as Brown Thomas or Arnotts. Advantage: range and quality. Disadvantage: higher prices.

Discount store: a store selling a limited range at low prices, kept low by minimal service and fast turnover of stock (goods sell quickly and are replaced), such as Dealz or Aldi. Advantage: low price. Disadvantage: limited choice.

Mail-order or online retailer: sells from a catalogue or website and delivers to the consumer's home, such as ASOS. Advantage: convenience and easy price comparison. Disadvantage: goods cannot be examined first and delivery takes time.
Market stall or farmers' market: small-scale direct selling, often by producers, typically of fresh produce.
Independent retailers compete on personal service and specialist knowledge, while chains and supermarkets compete on range and price.
notes.tip: A classification question wants the class name plus one named store per class, so do not give two outlets of the same class. Aldi fits both a chain and a discount store, so say which class you mean. For an outlet question, give the class, an example, then one advantage and one disadvantage as separate points.

notes.h: Choosing an outlet for an appliance (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Buying an appliance such as a washing machine is a big purchase, so the outlet matters as much as the product. A shopper compares outlets on more than the price tag.
points: Price: compare the cost of the same item in different outlets, since discount and online sellers may charge less than a department store.
Range: a wider range lets you compare several models before you decide.
Advice and demonstration: staff in a shop can explain features and show the appliance working, which an online seller cannot do.
After-sales service: whether the outlet will install, service and repair the appliance, which matters if it breaks down.
Delivery: whether the outlet delivers the appliance, how soon, and whether it charges for this.
Guarantee and returns policy: whether the appliance is covered if it is faulty and whether the outlet takes it back, so you are protected if it is not right.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name two outlets for buying an appliance and give one advantage and one disadvantage of each. Tie each advantage and disadvantage to one of these factors, such as price or advice.

notes.b: Retailers design the shopping environment around how people perceive value, risk and time. Understanding these tactics helps a consumer spend on purpose rather than on impulse.
points: Impulse buying: an unplanned purchase triggered by a display, a special offer or a product seen at the checkout.
Perceived value: shoppers judge a price against a reference price, so a 'was/now' price or a multi-buy makes a reduction seem a bargain even when the saving is small.
Mood and environment: music, aroma, lighting and layout keep shoppers relaxed. Relaxed shoppers browse for longer and so see and buy more products.
Perceived risk: consumers hesitate over unfamiliar products, so a known brand reduces the risk they feel in buying.
Limited time and attention: shoppers rely on quick cues such as brand, colour, packaging and price rather than reading every label.
Scarcity and urgency: labels such as 'limited offer' encourage a purchase now rather than later.
Social proof: displays showing many units, or a 'best seller' label, suggest that other people approve of the product.
Consumer's response: separate needs from wants, then use a shopping list and a budget to reduce impulse spending.
notes.tip: Link the shopper's reaction to the retailer's action: a was/now price makes the reduction look larger, so shoppers buy now. Merchandising techniques such as layout and shelf position are only causes of behaviour here, not the focus of the answer.

notes.h: Changes in shopping patterns (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Shopping patterns have changed in response to time pressure, technology and changing values. For each change, be ready to say what changed and why shoppers or retailers changed.
points: Frequency: many households have moved from a single weekly bulk shop to several smaller top-up trips.
One-stop shopping: large out-of-town centres and retail parks sell food, clothing and services under one roof, alongside local shops.
Extended hours: late-night, Sunday and 24-hour opening give shoppers more flexibility, which suits people with long working hours.
Online, television and social media shopping: consumers order through websites, apps, TV shopping channels and social media, often with home delivery.
Self-checkout and scan-as-you-go systems let shoppers bypass the checkout queue and help retailers cut staff costs. Loyalty apps also record buying habits.
Resale and second-hand trade: charity shops, vintage stores and online resale platforms have grown as shoppers seek value and reduce waste.
Drivers of change: time pressure, working patterns, household structure, technology, budget, health and special diets, and environmental and ethical concern.
notes.tip: An analysis question wants at least five developed points, such as payment methods, apps and loyalty, self-checkout, frequency, large centres, opening hours, online and social shopping, and resale. Develop each one with a reason rather than just naming it.

notes.b: How people pay has changed as well as where they shop. Each method can be judged on convenience, security, cost and record keeping.
points: Cash: widely accepted and carries no interest, but it can be lost or stolen and gives few records of what you spent.
Debit card: contactless and convenient, and it spends funds from your own account without interest, but it depends on funds being in the account and on technology working.
Contactless and mobile payment: tapping a card or paying with a phone app, along with debit cards, has largely replaced cash, because it is quick at the till.
Credit card: lets you buy now and pay later, but the amount spent must be repaid.
notes.tip: To evaluate a payment method, name it, give one feature that helps the consumer, and give one weakness such as security, interest, or reliance on funds or technology.

notes.h: Consumer research: desk and field research (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Consumer research gathers information about what consumers want, how they buy, and how large a market is. The two types are separated by who collects the data: existing information against new information.
points: Purpose: research identifies consumer wants and expectations, tests the market before a product is launched or developed, and highlights trends, market size and potential markets.
Desk research uses existing (secondary) information, meaning data someone else has already gathered, such as reports from state agencies, Central Statistics Office data and internet sources.
Desk research is quick to carry out, relatively inexpensive, and can cover a large amount of information.
Desk research may be general or out of date, so it shows what people do rather than why, and it may not answer a specific question about a product.
Field research collects new (primary) information directly from consumers, through questionnaires, surveys, interviews, observation, vox pops, consumer panels and focus groups.
Field research is specific and up to date, showing attitudes, preferences and reasons for buying, but it takes longer and costs more.
A vox pop is a short, informal interview with members of the public in a public place, used to gather opinions quickly.
A consumer panel is a fixed group of consumers who report on products over time; a focus group is a guided discussion with a small group about a product.
Loyalty card data and application forms record buying habits and personal details, which retailers use as a research source.
notes.tip: Always say who collects the data (existing sources or the researcher), give two examples of each type, and add one benefit and one drawback. Desk research is any existing data, including internet and CSO figures, not just the library; field research is primary data collected for the question in hand.

notes.h: Uses of consumer research (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Research benefits the retailer, the manufacturer and the consumer, because each needs to know what people will buy.
points: Retailer: research identifies the type of person likely to buy a product.
Retailer: research shows whether a product meets consumer requirements, and shows the size and location of the market.
Manufacturer: research shows what consumers will buy before production is committed, so money is not wasted on products that will not sell.
Consumer: research identifies what consumers need, so that products can be improved in quality and matched to those needs.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name three research methods and give one benefit to the retailer and one to the consumer. Give the consumer benefit as products improved in quality and matched to need.

keyTerms.definition: A single, locally owned shop offering personal service and a specialised range.
One of several outlets under the same ownership, selling a standard range and buying in bulk.
A large store divided into departments that sell clothing, household goods and cosmetics.
A store selling a limited range at low prices, kept low by minimal service and fast stock turnover.
The worth a shopper attaches to a price, judged against a reference price such as a previous or recommended price.
The uncertainty a consumer feels about whether a product will meet expectations, which makes unfamiliar products harder to buy.
The collection of existing information from published or online sources, such as state agency reports.
The collection of new information directly from consumers through observation, interviews and surveys.
Information collected for the first time for a specific purpose, such as a survey carried out by the researcher.
Information that already exists and was collected for another purpose, such as census or government figures.
A short, informal interview with a member of the public, used to gather quick opinions.
A guided discussion with a small group of consumers about a product, service or advertisement.

factCards.term: Three advantages of gathering information from published sources
factCards.definition: Large amounts of information can be collected quickly, it is relatively inexpensive, and it needs no direct contact with consumers.

factCards.term: Three limitations of relying on published sources for market information
factCards.definition: The information is general rather than detailed, it is quantitative so it shows what people do rather than why, and it may not answer a specific question about a product.

factCards.term: Four methods of collecting new information from consumers
factCards.definition: Observation, interviews, surveys and vox pops.

factCards.term: Three benefits of research to a retailer
factCards.definition: It identifies the type of person likely to buy, shows whether a product meets requirements, and shows the size and location of the market.
A self-service layout and a wide range of food and household goods.

factCards.term: Irish state body whose data is a common source for desk research

questions.prompt: Describe the main features of two classes of retail outlet, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Two classes, each with a feature and an example. Independent retailer: a single, locally owned shop with personal service and a specialist range, such as a butcher or jeweller. Department store: a large store divided into departments selling clothing, household goods and cosmetics, such as Brown Thomas. Other acceptable answers include supermarket, chain store, discount store and mail-order or online retailer, each with a correct feature and a correct example.

questions.prompt: Analyse how changes in shopping patterns affect consumers and retailers, and explain how consumer research helps a retailer respond to these changes.
questions.model: Changes in shopping patterns: more frequent top-up trips, one-stop shopping in large centres, extended and 24-hour opening, online, television and social media shopping with home delivery, cashless payment and self-checkout, and growth of resale. Effects on consumers: more choice and convenience, but greater risk of overspending and of payment fraud online. Effects on retailers: need to offer online ordering and delivery, to extend hours, and to compete on range and convenience, while smaller independent shops may lose trade. Consumer research: desk research uses existing data, such as state agency reports and Central Statistics Office figures, to show market trends and size quickly and cheaply; field research uses surveys, interviews, focus groups and consumer panels to find out why consumers are changing their habits. Together they show a retailer which products to stock, what type of customer to target, and where to locate or sell. A complete answer links each change to a consumer or retailer effect and shows how a named research method would reveal it.
